p.src: Now the crown prince of the Kingdom of Black Rooster, having parted from the Great Sage, soon returned to the city. As expected, he did not head for the audience gate or dare have his return announced, but went straight to the rear palace gate, where he found several eunuchs standing guard. Seeing the crown prince approach, they dared not hinder him and let him pass. The fine prince urged his horse forward and charged inside, soon arriving beneath the Pavilion of Brocade Fragrance. There he saw the chief queen seated in the pavilion, with dozens of consorts on either side holding fans, while she leaned against the carved railing and wept. Why, you may ask, was she weeping? It turned out that during the fourth watch she too had dreamed a dream; half of it she remembered and half remained vague, and she sat deep in thought.

p.src: The crown prince dismounted, knelt below the pavilion, and called, “Mother.” The queen forced her face into a joyful expression and cried, “My child, what happiness! What happiness! For the past two or three years you have been attending lectures with your royal father in the front hall, and I have been unable to see you; how greatly I have missed you. How did you find the leisure to visit me today? It is truly a boundless joy! Truly a boundless joy! My child, why does your voice sound so sorrowful? Your royal father is advanced in years. When one day the dragon returns to the blue sea and the phoenix to the crimson heavens, you will inherit the throne; what cause can you have for unhappiness?” The crown prince kowtowed and said, “Mother, let me ask you: who is it that ascended the dragon throne? Who, in truth, is the man who calls himself sovereign?” Hearing this, the queen said, “Has the child gone mad? The emperor is your royal father. Why do you ask?” The crown prince kowtowed and said, “I earnestly beg you, Mother, to pardon your son; only then shall I dare ask. If you will not pardon me, I dare not ask.” The queen said, “What guilt could there be between mother and son? I pardon you, I pardon you. Speak quickly.” The crown prince said, “Mother, I ask you this: were matters between husband and wife in the palace three years ago the same as the affection shown during the three years since, or were they different?” At these words the queen was frightened out of her wits. She hurried down from the pavilion, raised him up, clasped him tightly to her breast, and said with tears falling from her eyes, “My child, you and I have not seen each other for so long; why have you come to the palace today to ask me this?” The crown prince said angrily, “Mother, if you have something to say, say it quickly. If you do not, a great matter will be delayed.” Only then did the queen dismiss all attendants. p.src: On hearing this, the crown prince pulled free, seized the saddle, and mounted his horse. The queen caught hold of him and said, “My child, what business can be so urgent that you leave before our talk is finished?” The crown prince knelt before her and said, “Mother, I dared not tell you. At this morning’s court I received an imperial command to take hawks and hounds outside the city to hunt. By chance I met a holy scripture-seeking monk sent by the emperor of the Eastern Land. His senior disciple is Sun the Pilgrim, who is exceedingly skilled at subduing demons. It turns out that my royal father died in the octagonal glazed well in the imperial garden, and this creature, wholly false, transformed itself into him and usurped the dragon throne. During the third watch last night, my royal father appeared to him in a dream and asked him to come into the city to capture the monster. Your son did not dare believe it all, so I came especially to ask you, Mother. But after what you have just said, he must indeed be a demon.” The queen said, “My son, how can you accept an outsider’s words as truth so readily?” The crown prince replied, “I still dared not take it as certain, but my royal father left him a token.” The queen asked what it was. The crown prince took the gold-mounted white jade tablet from his sleeve and handed it to her. The queen recognized it as the king’s former treasure, and tears gushed from her eyes like a spring. She cried, “My lord, why, after being dead for three years, did you not come to see me, but first appeared to the holy monk and then to the crown prince?” The crown prince asked, “Mother, what do you mean by that?” The queen said, “My son, during the fourth watch I too dreamed a dream. I saw your royal father standing before me drenched in water, and he told me himself that he was dead, that his ghost had entreated the Tang Monk to subdue the false emperor and restore his former body. I remember that those were his words, but half of them remained indistinct. I was sitting here in doubt, never imagining that you would come today with the same story and bring out this treasure as well. I shall keep it for now. Go and ask that holy monk to act without delay. If he truly sweeps away the demonic miasma and distinguishes evil from righteousness, you may thereby repay the kindness with which your royal father raised you.”

p.src: The crown prince hurriedly mounted, went out through the rear palace gate, and slipped away from the city. Truly, with tears in his eyes he kowtowed farewell to the queen mother, and bearing grief he bowed his head to return to the Tang Monk. Before long he passed through the city gate, rode straight to the entrance of Baolin Monastery, and dismounted. The soldiers received the crown prince, while the red orb of the sun was already about to sink. The crown prince ordered that none of the soldiers was to stir recklessly. He then entered the monastery gate alone, straightened his robes and cap, and respectfully asked to see the Pilgrim. The Monkey King came swaggering out of the main hall. The crown prince fell to both knees and said, “Master, I have returned.” The Pilgrim stepped forward, helped him up, and said, “Please rise. When you entered the city, did you question anyone?” The crown prince replied, “I went to question my mother.” He then recounted everything that had been said. The Pilgrim smiled faintly and said, “If he is as cold as that, I suppose some sort of icy thing must have transformed itself into him. It is nothing serious, nothing serious. Let old Sun sweep it away for you. Only it is late today, and the deed cannot conveniently be done. Go back first, and I shall come tomorrow morning.” The crown prince knelt and kowtowed, saying, “Master, I shall remain here, wait upon you until tomorrow, and then go with you.” The Pilgrim said, “That will not do, that will not do. If I enter the city together with you, the monster will grow suspicious. Instead of thinking that I happened to meet you, he will say that you invited old Sun. Would that not make him turn against you?” The crown prince said, “Even if I enter the city now, he will blame me.” The Pilgrim asked, “Why would he blame you?” The crown prince replied, “At morning court I was ordered to lead a great company of men, horses, hawks, and hounds outside the city, yet after a whole day we have not taken a single wild creature. How can I present myself before His Majesty? If he charges me with incompetence and imprisons me in Youli, what support will you have when you enter the city tomorrow? Besides, among all the officials at court, I have not a single trusted friend.” The Pilgrim said, “Why should that matter? Had you told me earlier, could I not have found some game for you?”

p.src: What a Great Sage! Right there before the crown prince he displayed his powers, sprang upward, and leaped into the clouds. He formed a spell with his fingers and recited the true words “Om, Purify the Dharma Realm,” compelling the mountain and earth gods to appear in midair and salute him, saying, “Great Sage, why has Your Honour summoned these humble gods? What are your commands?” The Pilgrim said, “Old Sun has escorted the Tang Monk here and wishes to capture an evil demon, but unfortunately the crown prince has taken no game on his hunt and dares not return to court. I ask a favour of you: quickly find some river deer, musk deer, deer, rabbits, beasts, and birds, and bring them here so that he may return.” Hearing this, the mountain and earth gods dared not disobey, but asked how many of each he required. The Great Sage replied, “The number does not matter. Just bring some.” The gods at once ordered the spirit soldiers of their districts to raise a beast-gathering spectral wind. They caught wild fowl and pheasants, antlered deer and plump river deer, foxes, badgers, raccoon dogs, rabbits, tigers, leopards, wolves, and other creatures—over a thousand in all—and presented them to the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim said, “Old Sun does not want them. Twist all their sinews so that they cannot move, and lay them separately along both sides of the forty-li road. Then those men can capture them without releasing their hawks and hounds and take them back to the city. That shall count as your service.” The gods obeyed, withdrew the spectral wind, and laid the creatures out on both sides of the road.

p.src: Only then did the Pilgrim bring his cloud down and say to the prince, “Your Highness, please return. There is already game along the road; gather it up yourself.” Seeing him wield such divine powers in midair, how could the prince disbelieve him? He could only kowtow and take his leave. He went out through the monastery gate, gave the order, and had the soldiers return to the city. Sure enough, countless wild creatures lay beside the road. Without even loosing their hawks and hounds, the soldiers seized them one after another with their bare hands and cheered, all declaring that it was due to His Highness’s great good fortune, never guessing that it was Old Sun’s divine power. Hear how they sang their victory songs as they surged back into the city.

p.src: The Pilgrim, meanwhile, remained to protect Tripitaka. When the monks of the monastery saw how close the travelers were with the prince, how could they fail to treat them respectfully? They prepared another vegetarian meal, entertained the Tang Monk, and lodged him once more in the meditation hall. As the first watch drew near, the Pilgrim had matters on his mind and could not fall asleep. He rolled to his feet, went to the Tang Monk’s bedside, and called, “Master.” The elder had not yet fallen asleep, but knowing that the Pilgrim was forever making alarming commotions, he pretended to sleep and did not answer. The Pilgrim felt for his bald head and shook it wildly, saying, “Master, how can you be asleep?” The Tang Monk said angrily, “You impudent creature! Why are you still awake at this hour, and what are you shouting about?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, there is a matter I should discuss with you.” The elder asked, “What matter?” The Pilgrim said, “During the day I boasted to that prince that my powers were higher than the mountains and deeper than the sea, and that capturing the fiend would be as easy as taking something from my own pocket: I need only reach out and bring him back. Yet I cannot sleep either; now that I think it over, the business presents certain difficulties.” The Tang Monk said, “If you say it is difficult, then simply do not capture him.” The Pilgrim said, “I must still capture him; it is only that the legal grounds are unsound.” The Tang Monk said, “What nonsense, you monkey! The fiend has usurped a sovereign’s throne; how can you call the grounds unsound?” The Pilgrim replied, “Venerable Master, you know only how to recite sutras, worship the Buddha, sit in meditation, and contemplate Chan. When have you ever studied the laws of Xiao He? As the common saying goes, ‘To catch a thief, catch him with the stolen goods.’ That monster has been emperor for three years without once giving himself away or letting the secret leak. He has shared the beds of the consorts and empress in the three palaces and enjoyed himself with both ranks of civil and military officials. Even if Old Sun has the ability to seize him, it would be hard to name a charge against him.” The Tang Monk asked, “Why would it be hard to charge him?” The Pilgrim replied, “Even a gourd without a mouth would roll about a few times before you. He might well say, ‘I am the king of the Kingdom of Black Rooster. What offense against Heaven have I committed that you should come to arrest me?’ What documentary proof could we produce to argue the case with him?”

p.src: The Tang Monk said, “Then decide for yourself how to handle it.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Old Sun’s plan is already complete. The only obstacle is that you, Venerable Master, are somewhat inclined to play favorites.” The Tang Monk asked, “How do I play favorites?” The Pilgrim said, “Bajie is clumsy and dull, yet you show him a little partiality.” The Tang Monk said, “How am I partial to him?” The Pilgrim said, “If you are not partial to him, then be a little bolder now and remain here with Friar Sand. Let Old Sun take Bajie into the city of Black Rooster tonight. We shall find the imperial garden, open the crystal-glass well, haul up the emperor’s corpse, and wrap it in our baggage cloth. When we enter the city tomorrow, never mind exchanging travel documents: as soon as I see the monster, I shall draw my cudgel and strike. If he says anything, we shall show him the skeleton and say, ‘This is the man you murdered.’ Then we shall have the prince come forward to mourn his father, the empress come out to identify her husband, and all the civil and military officials behold their sovereign; after that, Old Sun and his brothers will set to work. Only then shall we have a lawsuit with an opposing party, fit to be tried.” Hearing this, the Tang Monk was secretly delighted, but said, “I fear Bajie may refuse to go.” The Pilgrim laughed. “There, you see? I said you favored him. How do you know already that he will refuse? When I call you, just pretend not to answer, as you did before, for half an hour—that will suffice. Once I go, with this incorruptible three-inch tongue of mine, let alone Zhu Bajie—even Zhu Nine-Precepts could be made to follow me.” The Tang Monk said, “Very well. Go and call him as you please.”

p.src: Leaving his master, the Pilgrim went straight to Bajie’s bedside and called, “Bajie! Bajie!” The fool was weary from traveling; the moment he laid down his head, he did nothing but snore, and no calling could wake him. The Pilgrim seized his ear and grabbed his bristles, then gave such a pull that he hauled him upright, calling again, “Bajie!” The fool still struggled in a sleepy daze. The Pilgrim called once more, and the fool said, “Go to sleep. Stop fooling around—we have to travel tomorrow.” The Pilgrim said, “I am not fooling around. There is a piece of business I want you to undertake with me.” Bajie asked, “What sort of business?” The Pilgrim said, “Did you hear what that prince said?” Bajie replied, “I never met him and did not hear a word he said.” The Pilgrim said, “The prince told me that the fiend possesses a treasure which gives him courage enough to withstand ten thousand men. When we enter the city tomorrow, we cannot avoid fighting him. If the monster brings out that treasure and subdues us, would that not turn a fine affair into a sorry one? It occurred to me that if one cannot beat a man, it is best to strike first. Would it not be well for you and me to go steal his treasure first?” Bajie said, “Brother, you are coaxing me into becoming a thief! Still, this is a piece of business I could undertake. Since I know exactly what help you need, let me make my terms clear: once we have stolen the treasure and subdued the fiend, I will not suffer any petty, stingy division of the spoils. I want the treasure for myself.” The Pilgrim asked, “What do you want it for?” Bajie replied, “I am not as clever or eloquent as the rest of you, able to beg a vegetarian meal wherever people are found. Old Hog is heavy-bodied and coarse of speech, and cannot recite sutras. If I reach some helpless, barren place, I could trade it for food.” The Pilgrim said, “Old Sun seeks only fame; why would I covet any treasure? You may have it.” When the fool heard that it would all be his, his heart filled with joy. He rolled to his feet, put on his clothes, and set off with the Pilgrim. Indeed, clear wine reddens a man’s face, and yellow gold stirs even a seeker’s heart.

Since I know exactly what help you need, let me make my terms clear: once we have stolen the treasure and subdued the fiend, I will not suffer any petty, stingy division of the spoils. I want the treasure for myself.”
The Pilgrim asked, “What do you want it for?”
Bajie replied, “I am not as clever or eloquent as the rest of you, able to beg a vegetarian meal wherever people are found.
Old Hog is heavy-bodied and coarse of speech, and cannot recite sutras. If I reach some helpless, barren place, I could trade it for food.”
The Pilgrim said, “Old Sun seeks only fame; why would I covet any treasure?
You may have it.”
When the fool heard that it would all be his, his heart filled with joy. He rolled to his feet, put on his clothes, and set off with the Pilgrim.
Indeed, clear wine reddens a man’s face, and yellow gold stirs even a seeker’s heart.

p.src: The two quietly opened the door, slipped away from Tripitaka, mounted their auspicious radiance, and sped straight toward the city. Before long they arrived and lowered their clouds, just as the watchtower sounded the second watch. The Pilgrim said, “Brother, it is already the second watch.” Bajie said, “Excellent, excellent! Everyone is now deep in the first sleep of the night.” Instead of heading for the main southern gate, the two went straight to the rear palace gate, where they heard the clappers and bells sounding. The Pilgrim said, “Brother, both the front and rear gates are under strict guard. How are we to enter?” Bajie replied, “Who ever heard of thieves going through the gate? We need only vault over the wall.” Following his advice, the Pilgrim sprang up and landed atop the inner city wall. Bajie jumped up after him. The two slipped inside, found their way through the passages, and went straight in search of the imperial garden.

p.src: Wukong said, “Bajie, get to work. The treasure is buried beneath the plantain tree.” The fool raised his rake in both hands and knocked down the plantain tree. Then he rooted with his snout, digging three or four feet deep, until he uncovered a stone slab laid over something. Delighted, the fool said, “Brother, what luck! There really is treasure here, covered by a stone slab. I wonder whether it is stored in a jar or packed in a chest.” Wukong said, “Lift it and see.” The fool duly shoved the slab aside with his snout. When he looked, he saw a brilliant rosy radiance and a distinct white glow. Bajie laughed and said, “What luck, what luck! The treasure is giving off light.” But when he moved closer and looked carefully—ah! It was only the light of the stars and moon making the water in the well shine. Bajie said, “Brother, whenever you set about something, you always leave a loose end.” Wukong said, “What loose end have I left?” Bajie said, “This is a well. If you had told me back at the monastery that the treasure was in a well, I would have brought the two ropes used to tie our bundles, so that we could devise some way to lower old Pig down there. Now that we have come empty-handed, how am I to get down there and bring up whatever is inside?” Wukong said, “You mean to go down?” Bajie said, “That is exactly what I mean to do, but we have no rope.” Wukong laughed and said, “Take off your clothes, and I’ll show you a way.” Bajie said, “What fine clothes do I have anyway? I need only take off this robe.”

p.src: The Great Sage took out his gold-banded cudgel, pulled it at both ends, and cried, “Grow!” It grew fully seventy or eighty feet long. He said, “Bajie, hold on to one end, and I’ll lower you into the well.” Bajie said, “Brother, lower me if you will, but stop as soon as I reach the water.” Wukong said, “I understand.” The fool embraced the iron cudgel, and Wukong lightly lifted him and lowered him into the well. Before long, he reached the water. Bajie called, “I’ve reached the water.” Hearing him, Wukong thrust the cudgel downward. With a great splash, the fool plunged headfirst into the water and let go of the cudgel. Floating there, he spluttered and shouted, “That accursed ape! I told him to stop at the water, but he pushed me straight in.” Wukong drew up his cudgel and asked with a laugh, “Brother, is there any treasure?” Bajie said, “What treasure could I see? There is nothing but a well full of water.” Wukong said, “The treasure lies submerged at the bottom. Dive down and feel around for it.” The fool was indeed thoroughly at home in the water. He took a deep breath and plunged down. Ah! The bottom of that well was exceedingly deep. He plunged down in earnest once more and, opening his eyes, suddenly saw an ornamental gateway bearing the three characters “Crystal Palace.” Greatly alarmed, Bajie said, “This is terrible! I must have taken a wrong turn and stumbled into the sea. There is a Crystal Palace in the sea, but how could there be one inside a well?” Bajie did not realize that this was the Crystal Palace of the Dragon King of the Well.

p.src: While Bajie was speaking to himself, a yaksha patrolling the waters opened the gate. On seeing his appearance, the creature hurried back inside to report: “Disaster, Your Majesty! A long-snouted, large-eared monk has fallen down from the mouth of the well. He is soaking wet and completely naked, yet he is still alive and is even speaking by magic.” When the Dragon King of the Well suddenly heard this, he was greatly startled and said, “That must be Marshal Tianpeng. Last night the Night-Roaming Deity came bearing an imperial decree to take the spirit of the King of the Kingdom of Black Rooster to visit Tang Sanzang and ask the Great Sage Equal to Heaven to subdue the demon. This must mean that the Great Sage Equal to Heaven and Marshal Tianpeng have arrived. We must not slight him. Hurry and welcome him in.”

p.src: The Dragon King straightened his robes and cap, led out his aquatic subjects, and called loudly at the gate, “Marshal Tianpeng, please come inside and take a seat.” Only then did Bajie brighten up and say, “So it is an old acquaintance.” Without caring whether it was proper or not, the fool went straight into the Crystal Palace. In truth he had no sense of rank or decorum; soaking wet and naked, he seated himself in the place of honor. The Dragon King said, “Marshal, I recently heard that your life was spared, that you took refuge in the Buddhist faith, and that you are protecting Tang Sanzang on his journey west to fetch the scriptures. How have you come to this place?” Bajie said, “That is exactly what brings me here. My elder brother Sun Wukong sends you his respectful greetings and has ordered me to come and ask you for some treasure.” The Dragon King said, “Alas, how could there be any treasure in a place like mine? I cannot compare with the Dragon Kings of the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers, who soar through the heavens, transform at will, and possess treasures. I have long been confined here and cannot even see the sun and moon for any length of time. From where, then, could any treasure possibly come?” Bajie said, “Do not make excuses. If you have one, bring it out.” The Dragon King said, “I do indeed have one treasure, but it cannot be brought out. How would it be if you, Marshal, came to see it yourself?” Bajie said, “Excellent, excellent, excellent! I must certainly go and see it.”

p.src: The Dragon King led the way, and the fool followed behind. After they had passed around the crystal palace, he saw a six-foot body lying beneath the covered gallery. Pointing with his hand, the Dragon King said, “Marshal, there lies the treasure.” Bajie stepped forward and looked. Ah! It was the body of an emperor, wearing a sky-soaring crown, an ocher-yellow robe, Carefree Shoes, and a Lantian jade belt, lying there stiff and straight. Bajie laughed. “No, no, no! That cannot be called a treasure. When old Pig was a monster in the mountains, I often ate such things for dinner. Never mind how many I saw—I ate more than I could count. How could this be called a treasure?” The Dragon King said, “Marshal, you do not understand. This is the corpse of the King of the Kingdom of Black Rooster. Since he fell into the well, I have preserved his features with a Face-Fixing Pearl, so his body has never decayed. If you will carry him out to the Great Sage Equaling Heaven, there may be some hope of restoring him to life. Then, never mind a treasure—you may have whatever you ask for.” Bajie said, “If that is so, I will carry him out for you—but how much burial money will you give me?” The Dragon King said, “In truth, I have no money.” Bajie said, “You mean to make a man work for nothing? If you truly have no money, I will not carry him.” The Dragon King said, “If you will not, then please be on your way.” Bajie turned to leave. The Dragon King ordered two powerful yakshas to carry the corpse out. They took it beyond the gate of the crystal palace, dropped it there, and removed the Water-Repelling Pearl; at once the waters roared in.

p.src: Bajie hurriedly looked back, but the gate of the crystal palace had vanished. His hand struck the emperor’s corpse, and terror made his legs weak and his sinews numb. He burst to the surface, clung to the wall of the well, and cried, “Brother, lower your staff and save me!” Wukong said, “Did you find a treasure?” Bajie replied, “There was no treasure. There was only a Dragon King of the Well down below, who told me to carry a dead man. I refused, so he sent me out through the gate. Then the crystal palace vanished, and all I could feel was that corpse. It frightened me so badly that my hands went limp and my sinews numb; I cannot struggle another inch. Brother, whatever else happens, please save me!” Wukong said, “That is the treasure. Why did you not carry him up?” Bajie said, “Who knows how long he has been dead? Why should I carry him?” Wukong said, “If you will not carry him, I am going back.” Bajie asked, “Where are you going back to?” Wukong said, “Back to the monastery, to sleep beside Master.” Bajie said, “And I am not going with you?” Wukong replied, “If you can climb up, I will take you along; if you cannot, then that is the end of it.” Bajie panicked. “How could I possibly climb? Just think—even a city wall is hard to scale. This well is broad in the belly and narrow at the mouth, with sheer circular walls. No water has been drawn from it for years, so it is covered all around with moss and terribly slippery. How am I to climb it? Brother, do not spoil the harmony between us. Wait—I will carry him up.” Wukong said, “That is more like it. Hurry and carry him up, and then we shall go back to sleep.” The fool plunged down once more, found the corpse, dragged it over, hoisted it onto his back, burst to the surface, and, bracing himself against the wall, said, “Brother, I have him on my back.” Wukong opened his eyes wide and saw that the corpse truly was on Bajie’s back; only then did he lower the gold-banded staff to the bottom of the well. The fool, now thoroughly vexed, opened his mouth and bit down on the iron staff, and Wukong lifted him out with ease.

p.src: Bajie set down the corpse, fished out his clothes, and put them on. When Wukong looked at the emperor, he saw that his features were unchanged, exactly as they had been in life. Wukong said, “Brother, this man has been dead for three years. How can his features still be undecayed?” Bajie said, “You do not know. The Dragon King of the Well told me that he had preserved him with a Face-Fixing Pearl, so the corpse has not decayed.” Wukong said, “What good fortune! What good fortune! First, his wrongs have yet to be redressed; second, it is destined that we should accomplish this deed. Brother, quickly carry him away.” Bajie asked, “Where am I to carry him?” Wukong replied, “Carry him to see Master.” Bajie muttered, “How did it come to this? How did it come to this? I was sleeping perfectly well, but this macaque coaxed me with his glib tongue into some supposed business, and now I am made to do a thing like this—carry a dead man. If I carry him, filthy water will drip down and soil my clothes, and no one will wash them for me. There are several patches on them already; when the weather turns damp, how am I to wear them?” Wukong said, “Just carry him to the monastery, and I will give you a change of clothes.” Bajie said, “Shameless liar! You do not even have a change for yourself, yet you will give one to me?” Wukong said, “If you are going to keep arguing, will you refuse to carry him?” Bajie replied, “I will not.” Wukong said, “Then stick out your shins and take twenty strokes.” Bajie panicked. “Brother, that staff is heavy. If you strike me twenty times, I shall be just like this emperor.” Wukong said, “If you fear a beating, put him on your back and be on your way at once.” Bajie truly was afraid of being beaten. In a foul temper, he dragged the corpse over, hoisted it onto his back, and strode out of the garden.

p.src: The Great Sage formed a spell with his fingers, recited an incantation, drew a breath from the southeast, and blew it forth. A violent gale arose, swept Bajie out of the palace’s inner court and carried them clear of the city. When the wind subsided, the two landed and continued slowly on their way. The fool was secretly resentful and plotted to avenge himself on Wukong. “This monkey has made sport of me. When we reach the monastery, I shall make sport of him. I will urge Master to insist that he can revive the man; and if he fails, Master will recite the Tight-Fillet Spell and squeeze the brains from this monkey’s skull. Only then shall I be satisfied.” As he walked, he thought it over again and again. “No, that will not do. If he is told to cure the man, it will be easy: he will go to King Yama’s house, fetch back the soul, and revive him. I shall say that he may not go to the underworld and must revive the man here in the world of the living. That will be the better plan.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, they reached the monastery gate. They went straight inside and dropped the corpse before the meditation hall. Bajie called, “Master, get up and see something strange!” The Tang Monk had been unable to sleep and was just telling Sha Monk how Wukong had tricked Bajie into going out and how neither had yet returned. Suddenly hearing Bajie call, the Tang Monk hastily rose and asked, “Disciple, what am I to see?” Bajie replied, “Wukong’s maternal grandfather. Old Pig was made to carry him here.” Wukong said, “You filthy, meal-stuffing fool! What maternal grandfather would I have?” Bajie said, “Brother, if he is not your maternal grandfather, why did you make old Pig carry him here? You have no idea how much strength it cost me.”

u.src: Before he had finished speaking, they reached the monastery gate. They went straight inside and dropped the corpse before the meditation hall.
Bajie called, “Master, get up and see something strange!”
The Tang Monk had been unable to sleep and was just telling Sha Monk how Wukong had tricked Bajie into going out and how neither had yet returned.
Suddenly hearing Bajie call, the Tang Monk hastily rose and asked, “Disciple, what am I to see?”
Bajie replied, “Wukong’s maternal grandfather. Old Pig was made to carry him here.”
Wukong said, “You filthy, meal-stuffing fool! What maternal grandfather would I have?”
Bajie said, “Brother, if he is not your maternal grandfather, why did you make old Pig carry him here?
You have no idea how much strength it cost me.”

p.src: When Tripitaka and Sha Monk opened the door and looked, they saw that the emperor's countenance was unchanged, as though he were still alive. The elder was suddenly overcome with sorrow and said, “Your Majesty, little did you know that an enemy from a former life would confront you in this one, secretly take your life, and force you to leave your wife and part from your son, while neither civil nor military officials knew what had happened, nor did any of your many officers understand. How pitiful that your wife and son remain in ignorance! Who has ever come to burn incense and offer you tea?” Then he broke down, and tears poured from his eyes like rain. Bajie laughed and said, “Master, what has his death to do with you? He is no father or ancestor of yours, so why weep for him?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, compassion is the foundation of those who have left the household, and helping others is their gateway. How can you be so hard-hearted?” Bajie said, “It is not that I am hard-hearted. Elder Brother told me he could bring him back to life; if he could not, I would never have carried the man here.” The elder was naturally as easily swayed as water, and once that fool had stirred him up, he called out, “Wukong, if you truly possess the means to restore this emperor to life, then indeed, ‘Saving one life is better than building a seven-storeyed pagoda.’ For us, that would be better even than worshipping the Buddha at Vulture Peak.” The Pilgrim said, “Master, why do you believe this fool's wild talk? When a person dies, after three sevens or five sevens—or at the latest, the full seven sevens of forty-nine days—once the punishment incurred in the world of the living has been discharged, the soul passes on to rebirth. He has now been dead for three years. How could he possibly be saved?” Hearing this, Tripitaka said, “Very well, then.” Bajie, bitterly resentful and unwilling to let the matter rest, said, “Master, do not let him deceive you. He has a touch of madness in his head. Just keep reciting that spell, and I guarantee he will give you back a living man.” And sure enough, Tripitaka began reciting the Tight-Fillet Spell, making the monkey's eyes bulge and his head throb with pain.
